stem: People applying to settle in the UK must also show they can speak and understand English.
options: *True | False
explanation: Most applicants for settlement or citizenship must pass the Life in the UK test and also meet the English language requirement.

stem: What do most people need to pass to settle permanently or become a British citizen?
options: *The Life in the UK test | A driving test | A university degree | A first aid course
explanation: Most adults applying for settlement or citizenship must pass the Life in the UK test. Some people, such as those over 65, do not need to take it.

stem: How many questions are there in the Life in the UK test?
explanation: The test has 24 multiple-choice questions and you have 45 minutes to answer them.
handbook_ref: Chapter 1 · Taking the Life in the UK test

stem: To pass the Life in the UK test you need to answer at least 75% of the questions correctly.
options: *True | False
explanation: The pass mark is 75%, which means at least 18 of the 24 questions must be right.
handbook_ref: Chapter 1 · Taking the Life in the UK test

stem: Which of these is a fundamental principle of British life?
options: *Democracy | Rule by the army | One religion for everyone | Rule by the richest families
explanation: Fundamental principles of British life include democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty and tolerance of different faiths and beliefs.
handbook_ref: Chapter 1 · The values and principles of the UK

stem: People in the UK are expected to respect the rights of others to hold their own opinions.
options: *True | False
explanation: Tolerance is a core British value. You can disagree with someone, but you should respect their right to their own views and beliefs.
handbook_ref: Chapter 1 · The values and principles of the UK

stem: Which TWO are responsibilities of people who live in the UK?
options: *Respect and obey the law | *Look after the area you live in | Join a political party | Go to a place of worship every week
explanation: Everyone should respect the law and look after themselves, their family and the area where they live. Joining a party or religion is a free choice.
handbook_ref: Chapter 1 · The values and principles of the UK

stem: Which of these is NOT part of the UK?
options: *The Republic of Ireland | Wales | Scotland | Northern Ireland
explanation: The UK is made up of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. The Republic of Ireland is a separate, independent country.

stem: Which countries make up Great Britain?
options: *England, Scotland and Wales | England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland | England and Wales only | England, Wales and Northern Ireland
explanation: Great Britain is the island of England, Scotland and Wales. The United Kingdom adds Northern Ireland.

stem: The Isle of Man is part of the UK.
options: True | *False
explanation: The Isle of Man and the Channel Islands are Crown dependencies. They have their own governments and are not part of the UK.

stem: Which TWO are Crown dependencies?
options: *The Channel Islands | *The Isle of Man | The Isle of Wight | Anglesey
explanation: The Channel Islands and the Isle of Man have a special link to the UK but run their own affairs. The Isle of Wight and Anglesey are part of the UK.

stem: What is the capital city of Wales?
options: *Cardiff | Swansea | Newport | Bangor
explanation: Cardiff is the capital city of Wales. The capital of England is London, of Scotland is Edinburgh and of Northern Ireland is Belfast.

stem: What is the capital city of Northern Ireland?
options: *Belfast | Londonderry | Armagh | Newry
explanation: Belfast is the capital of Northern Ireland. It is home to the Northern Ireland Assembly at Stormont.

stem: What is the capital city of Scotland?
options: *Edinburgh | Glasgow | Aberdeen | Dundee
explanation: Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland. Glasgow is Scotland's largest city, but it is not the capital.

stem: Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each have their own parliament or assembly with some powers of their own.
options: *True | False
explanation: Some powers are devolved from the UK Parliament, so Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland can make their own decisions on matters such as health and education.

stem: When did fighting in the First World War end?
options: *11 November 1918 | 6 June 1944 | 11 November 1914 | 8 May 1945
explanation: The First World War ended at 11 am on 11 November 1918. People remember those who died on this date each year.

stem: On the first day of which battle in 1916 did the British suffer about 60,000 casualties?
options: *The Battle of the Somme | The Battle of Britain | The Battle of Waterloo | The Battle of Hastings
explanation: The Battle of the Somme in 1916 was one of the bloodiest battles of the First World War, with huge losses on the first day.

stem: Who became Prime Minister in 1940 and led Britain in the Second World War?
options: *Winston Churchill | Clement Attlee | Neville Chamberlain | Margaret Thatcher
explanation: Winston Churchill became Prime Minister in 1940. His speeches helped people stay strong when Britain stood alone against Germany.

stem: Which battle was fought in the skies over Britain in 1940?
options: *The Battle of Britain | The Battle of the Somme | D-Day | The Battle of Trafalgar
explanation: In the Battle of Britain, the Royal Air Force defended the country using Spitfire and Hurricane aircraft, and stopped a German invasion.

stem: What happened on D-Day, 6 June 1944?
options: *Allied forces landed in Normandy | Germany surrendered | The Battle of Britain began | Soldiers were rescued from Dunkirk
explanation: On D-Day, Allied forces landed on the beaches of Normandy in France. This began the defeat of Germany in western Europe.

stem: Who discovered penicillin?
options: *Alexander Fleming | Frank Whittle | Alan Turing | Tim Berners-Lee
explanation: Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928. It was later developed into a medicine that treats many infections.

stem: In which year was the National Health Service (NHS) set up?
explanation: The NHS began in 1948 under the Labour government. Aneurin (Nye) Bevan, the Minister for Health, led its creation.

stem: In 1940, many British soldiers were rescued from the beaches of Dunkirk by small civilian boats.
options: *True | False
explanation: Over 300,000 soldiers were rescued from Dunkirk in France. People still talk about the 'Dunkirk spirit' when facing hard times together.

stem: Which mathematician's ideas helped lead to the modern computer?
options: *Alan Turing | Isaac Newton | John Logie Baird | Frank Whittle
explanation: Alan Turing was a British mathematician. His idea of the 'Turing machine' had a big influence on computer science.

stem: Who invented the jet engine?
options: *Sir Frank Whittle | Sir Robert Watson-Watt | John Logie Baird | Sir Christopher Cockerell
explanation: Sir Frank Whittle, a British engineer, developed the jet engine in the 1930s. Sir Robert Watson-Watt developed radar.

stem: Who led the Labour government that came to power in 1945?
options: *Clement Attlee | Winston Churchill | Harold Wilson | Tony Blair
explanation: Clement Attlee became Prime Minister in 1945. His government created the NHS and introduced a welfare state.

stem: Where is Stonehenge?
options: *Wiltshire | Orkney | Cornwall | Kent
explanation: Stonehenge is a famous prehistoric monument in Wiltshire, in the south-west of England. It was probably a special place for gatherings.

stem: Where is Skara Brae, a very well-preserved Stone Age village?
options: *Orkney | Shetland | The Isle of Skye | Anglesey
explanation: Skara Brae is on Orkney, off the north coast of Scotland. It is the best-preserved prehistoric village in northern Europe.

stem: In which year did the Romans, under Emperor Claudius, invade Britain?
explanation: Julius Caesar tried to invade in 55 BC but did not stay. The Romans returned under Emperor Claudius in AD 43 and ruled for about 400 years.

stem: Who was Boudicca?
options: *Queen of the Iceni, who fought the Romans | A Roman empress who ruled Britain | A Saxon queen who defeated the Vikings | The first queen of Scotland
explanation: Boudicca led the Iceni, a tribe in what is now eastern England, against the Romans. Her statue stands on Westminster Bridge in London.

stem: Why did the Romans build Hadrian's Wall?
options: *To keep out the Picts in the north | To defend against the Vikings | To mark the border with Wales | To protect London from the Saxons
explanation: Emperor Hadrian built the wall in the north of England to keep out the Picts, who were ancestors of the Scottish people.

stem: When did the Romans leave Britain?
explanation: The Roman army left Britain in AD 410 to defend other parts of the Roman Empire. They never returned.

stem: Which burial site in Suffolk held an Anglo-Saxon king, buried with treasure in a ship?
options: *Sutton Hoo | Skara Brae | Jorvik | Lindisfarne
explanation: Sutton Hoo in Suffolk is the burial place of an Anglo-Saxon king. He was buried with treasure and armour, all placed inside a ship.

stem: Who became the first Archbishop of Canterbury?
options: *St Augustine | St Patrick | St Columba | St David
explanation: St Augustine led missionaries from Rome who spread Christianity in the south of England. He became the first Archbishop of Canterbury.

stem: Where did the Vikings come from?
options: *Denmark and Norway | France and Spain | Germany and the Netherlands | Italy and Greece
explanation: The Vikings came from Denmark and Norway. They first visited Britain in AD 789 to raid coastal towns and take goods and slaves.

stem: In which year did William of Normandy win the Battle of Hastings?
explanation: William defeated and killed the English king, Harold, at the Battle of Hastings in 1066. The battle is shown on the Bayeux Tapestry.

stem: After the Norman Conquest, William had a record made of towns, villages and land in England, called the Domesday Book.
options: *True | False
explanation: The Domesday Book listed who owned land and what animals they had. It still exists and gives a picture of England after the Norman Conquest.

stem: Which Anglo-Saxon king united the kingdoms and defeated the Vikings?
options: *Alfred the Great | Kenneth MacAlpin | Harold | Cnut
explanation: Alfred the Great brought the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms together and defeated the Vikings. Many Vikings then settled in the east and north of England.

stem: Who is usually thought of as the first Prime Minister?
options: *Sir Robert Walpole | Winston Churchill | William Pitt | Oliver Cromwell
explanation: Sir Robert Walpole was the first politician to lead the government as Prime Minister. He held the post from 1721 to 1742.

stem: In 1746, Bonnie Prince Charlie's army was defeated at which battle?
options: *The Battle of Culloden | The Battle of Bosworth Field | The Battle of Bannockburn | The Battle of Waterloo
explanation: Charles Edward Stuart, known as Bonnie Prince Charlie, tried to take the throne. His army was defeated at Culloden in Scotland in 1746.

stem: Which Scottish poet wrote 'Auld Lang Syne'?
options: *Robert Burns | Walter Scott | Robert Louis Stevenson | Dylan Thomas
explanation: Robert Burns is Scotland's best-known poet. People around the world sing his song 'Auld Lang Syne' at New Year.

stem: Whose work on steam power helped drive the Industrial Revolution?
options: *James Watt | Richard Arkwright | Isambard Kingdom Brunel | Henry Bessemer
explanation: James Watt was a Scottish scientist. His improvements to steam power helped factories and machines develop quickly during the Industrial Revolution.

stem: In which year did it become illegal to trade slaves in British ships or ports?
explanation: Parliament ended the slave trade in 1807. In 1833 the Emancipation Act ended slavery across the British Empire.

stem: Which MP led the campaign in Parliament against the slave trade?
options: *William Wilberforce | Robert Walpole | Winston Churchill | Aneurin Bevan
explanation: William Wilberforce was an MP and a Christian who campaigned for many years to end the slave trade.

stem: In 1805, Admiral Nelson defeated the French and Spanish fleets at which battle?
options: *The Battle of Trafalgar | The Battle of Waterloo | The Battle of the Somme | The Battle of Agincourt
explanation: Admiral Nelson won the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805 but was killed in the battle. Nelson's Column in Trafalgar Square remembers him.

stem: Who defeated Napoleon at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815?
options: *The Duke of Wellington | Admiral Nelson | Oliver Cromwell | Robert Walpole
explanation: The Duke of Wellington defeated Napoleon at Waterloo in 1815. He later became Prime Minister.

stem: For about how long was Queen Victoria on the throne?
options: *Almost 64 years | About 30 years | About 45 years | Over 70 years
explanation: Queen Victoria reigned from 1837 to 1901, almost 64 years. During this time Britain became a powerful country with a large empire.

stem: Who is famous for her nursing work during the Crimean War?
options: *Florence Nightingale | Emmeline Pankhurst | Elizabeth Fry | Jane Austen
explanation: Florence Nightingale cared for wounded soldiers in the Crimean War. She later set up a school for nurses in London.

stem: Which engineer built the Great Western Railway?
options: *Isambard Kingdom Brunel | James Watt | Henry Bessemer | Richard Arkwright
explanation: Isambard Kingdom Brunel was a great engineer. He built the Great Western Railway, tunnels, bridges and steamships.

stem: Who led the suffragettes, who campaigned for women to have the vote?
options: *Emmeline Pankhurst | Florence Nightingale | Margaret Thatcher | Jane Austen
explanation: Emmeline Pankhurst set up the Women's Social and Political Union. Its members, called suffragettes, campaigned hard for women's right to vote.

stem: In 1928, women got the right to vote at 21, the same age as men.
options: *True | False
explanation: In 1918 women over 30 got the vote. Ten years later, in 1928, women could vote at 21, the same as men.

stem: Which Scottish king defeated the English at the Battle of Bannockburn in 1314?
options: *Robert the Bruce | Kenneth MacAlpin | James IV | Macbeth
explanation: Robert the Bruce defeated the English at Bannockburn in 1314. Scotland stayed unconquered by the English.

stem: What was the Black Death?
options: *A plague that killed about a third of people in England | A famine in Ireland in the 1840s | A long war between England and France | A great fire that destroyed London
explanation: The Black Death reached Britain in 1348. About one third of the population of England died, and a similar share in Scotland and Wales.

stem: Which king was made to agree to the Magna Carta in 1215?
options: *King John | Henry VIII | Richard III | Edward I
explanation: Nobles forced King John to agree to the Magna Carta in 1215. It showed that even the king had to obey the law.

stem: Which English king won the Battle of Agincourt in 1415?
options: *Henry V | Henry VIII | Edward III | Richard II
explanation: Henry V led the English to victory over the French at Agincourt in 1415, during the Hundred Years War.

stem: Which battle in 1485 ended the Wars of the Roses?
options: *The Battle of Bosworth Field | The Battle of Hastings | The Battle of Bannockburn | The Battle of Culloden
explanation: Henry Tudor defeated King Richard III at Bosworth Field in 1485. He became King Henry VII, the first Tudor king.

stem: Which TWO families fought each other in the Wars of the Roses?
options: *The House of Lancaster | *The House of York | The House of Stuart | The House of Windsor
explanation: The Wars of the Roses were fought between the House of Lancaster, whose symbol was a red rose, and the House of York, whose symbol was a white rose.

stem: Who wrote The Canterbury Tales?
options: *Geoffrey Chaucer | William Shakespeare | William Caxton | Robert Burns
explanation: Geoffrey Chaucer wrote The Canterbury Tales, poems about pilgrims travelling to Canterbury. It was one of the first books printed in England.

stem: William Caxton was the first person in England to print books using a printing press.
options: *True | False
explanation: William Caxton brought the printing press to England in the 15th century. This helped books in English reach many more people.

stem: The Hundred Years War was fought between England and which country?
options: *France | Spain | Scotland | The Netherlands
explanation: England fought a long series of wars with France, known as the Hundred Years War. It actually lasted 116 years.

stem: Who was the first woman to be Prime Minister of the UK?
options: *Margaret Thatcher | Barbara Castle | Shirley Williams | Betty Boothroyd
explanation: Margaret Thatcher became the UK's first woman Prime Minister in 1979. She led the government until 1990.

stem: In which year did the UK join the European Economic Community?
explanation: The UK joined the European Economic Community in 1973, after earlier attempts to join had been refused.

stem: Who invented the World Wide Web?
options: *Sir Tim Berners-Lee | Alan Turing | John Logie Baird | James Goodfellow
explanation: Sir Tim Berners-Lee, a British scientist, created the World Wide Web. Information was first shared on it in 1990.

stem: Which 1998 agreement helped bring peace to Northern Ireland?
options: *The Good Friday Agreement | The Act of Union | The Treaty of Rome | The Belfast Charter
explanation: The Good Friday Agreement of 1998 helped end years of conflict in Northern Ireland. It led to a new Northern Ireland Assembly.

stem: In which country of the UK was Dolly the sheep, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell, created?
options: *Scotland | Wales | England | Northern Ireland
explanation: Dolly the sheep was cloned in 1996 by scientists at the Roslin Institute near Edinburgh, Scotland.

stem: The first baby conceived by IVF, sometimes called a 'test-tube baby', was born in the UK in 1978.
options: *True | False
explanation: British doctors developed IVF treatment. The first IVF baby was born in Oldham, England, in 1978.

stem: Which supersonic airliner was developed by Britain and France?
options: *Concorde | The Spitfire | The Comet | The Hurricane
explanation: Concorde was a passenger aircraft that flew faster than the speed of sound. It first flew in 1969 and carried passengers from 1976 to 2003.

stem: Who invented the hovercraft?
options: *Sir Christopher Cockerell | Sir Frank Whittle | James Goodfellow | Sir Peter Mansfield
explanation: Sir Christopher Cockerell, a British engineer, invented the hovercraft in the 1950s.

stem: Who invented the cash machine, or ATM?
options: *James Goodfellow | John Logie Baird | James Watt | Tim Berners-Lee
explanation: James Goodfellow, a Scottish engineer, invented the cash machine in the 1960s.

stem: In the 1950s and 1960s, the UK encouraged workers from which places to come and help rebuild?
options: *The West Indies, India and Pakistan | Australia and New Zealand | Canada and the USA | France and Germany
explanation: There was a shortage of workers after the war. People came from the West Indies, India, Pakistan and later Bangladesh to work in the UK.

stem: After votes in 1997, Scotland and Wales got their own elected bodies, which began work in 1999.
options: *True | False
explanation: The Scottish Parliament and the Welsh Assembly (now the Senedd) were set up in 1999, with powers over matters such as health and education.

stem: Which king broke away from the Church of Rome?
options: *Henry VIII | Edward I | Charles II | James I
explanation: Henry VIII set up the Church of England when the Pope would not let him end his first marriage.

stem: Which of Henry VIII's wives gave birth to his only son, Edward?
options: *Jane Seymour | Anne Boleyn | Catherine of Aragon | Catherine Parr
explanation: Jane Seymour gave Henry VIII the son he wanted, who became Edward VI. She died soon after the birth.

stem: In 1588, which fleet did the English defeat?
options: *The Spanish Armada | The French navy | The Dutch fleet | The Viking fleet
explanation: The English defeated the Spanish Armada, a large fleet of ships sent to invade England and bring back the Catholic faith.

stem: Who was the monarch when the Spanish Armada was defeated?
options: *Elizabeth I | Mary I | Victoria | Anne
explanation: Elizabeth I was queen when the Spanish Armada was defeated in 1588. She was very popular and her reign is often remembered as a golden age.

stem: Where was William Shakespeare born?
options: *Stratford-upon-Avon | London | Oxford | Canterbury
explanation: William Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon, England, in 1564. Many people think he is the greatest writer in the English language.

stem: Which king of Scotland also became King of England in 1603?
options: *James VI | Charles I | Robert the Bruce | William III
explanation: When Elizabeth I died without children, James VI of Scotland became James I of England. He ruled both countries.

stem: Which king was executed in 1649 after the English Civil War?
options: *Charles I | Charles II | James II | Henry VIII
explanation: Charles I lost the Civil War against Parliament and was executed in 1649. England became a republic for a short time.

stem: In the English Civil War, what were supporters of the king called?
options: *Cavaliers | Roundheads | Jacobites | Puritans
explanation: Supporters of the king were called Cavaliers. Supporters of Parliament were called Roundheads.

stem: Who became Lord Protector after the English Civil War?
options: *Oliver Cromwell | Robert Walpole | Thomas Cromwell | William of Orange
explanation: Oliver Cromwell led the army of Parliament and ruled England as Lord Protector until he died in 1658.

stem: In which year was there a great fire in London?
explanation: The Great Fire of London in 1666 destroyed many buildings. Sir Christopher Wren designed the new St Paul's Cathedral.

stem: What was the Glorious Revolution of 1688?
options: *William of Orange became king with no fighting in England | Parliament got rid of the monarchy | Scotland and England joined together | Charles II came back from exile
explanation: Protestant leaders invited William of Orange to take the throne. James II fled to France and there was no fighting in England, so it was called glorious.

stem: The Act of Union of 1707 joined England and Scotland into the Kingdom of Great Britain.
options: *True | False
explanation: The Act of Union created the Kingdom of Great Britain. Scotland kept its own legal and education systems and its own church.

stem: Which law of 1679 protects people from being held in prison unlawfully?
options: *The Habeas Corpus Act | The Bill of Rights | The Magna Carta | The Act of Union
explanation: The Habeas Corpus Act means someone who is arrested must be brought before a court. This protects people from being held without a lawful reason.

stem: Where is the Proms, an eight-week summer season of classical music, mainly held?
options: *The Royal Albert Hall | Wembley Stadium | The O2 Arena | Covent Garden
explanation: The Proms is a summer season of classical concerts held mainly at the Royal Albert Hall in London. It has run since 1895.

stem: Who composed 'Pomp and Circumstance'?
options: *Sir Edward Elgar | Benjamin Britten | Henry Purcell | Andrew Lloyd Webber
explanation: Sir Edward Elgar wrote the 'Pomp and Circumstance' marches. One is often sung as 'Land of Hope and Glory'.

stem: Who wrote Oliver Twist?
options: *Charles Dickens | Thomas Hardy | Jane Austen | Sir Arthur Conan Doyle
explanation: Charles Dickens wrote many famous novels, including Oliver Twist and Great Expectations. They show the lives of poor people in the 19th century.

stem: Who created the detective Sherlock Holmes?
options: *Sir Arthur Conan Doyle | Ian Fleming | Charles Dickens | Thomas Hardy
explanation: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, a Scottish doctor and writer, created Sherlock Holmes, one of the best-known fictional detectives.

stem: Which prize is given each year to a contemporary British artist?
options: *The Turner Prize | The Man Booker Prize | A BAFTA | The Laurence Olivier Award
explanation: The Turner Prize is named after the painter J M W Turner and celebrates contemporary art. The Man Booker Prize is for fiction.

stem: Who designed St Paul's Cathedral after the Great Fire of London?
options: *Sir Christopher Wren | Sir Edwin Lutyens | Capability Brown | Henry Moore
explanation: Sir Christopher Wren rebuilt St Paul's Cathedral and many London churches after the fire of 1666.

stem: The Eisteddfod is a Welsh festival of music, poetry and performance.
options: *True | False
explanation: The National Eisteddfod of Wales is a large festival of music, literature and performance, with many events in the Welsh language.

stem: Who wrote Pride and Prejudice?
options: *Jane Austen | Thomas Hardy | Charles Dickens | Agatha Christie
explanation: Jane Austen wrote Pride and Prejudice and Sense and Sensibility. Her novels are about marriage and family life.

stem: When is Boxing Day?
options: *26 December | 24 December | 1 January | 31 December
explanation: Boxing Day is the day after Christmas Day, 26 December. It is a public holiday.

stem: What is New Year's Eve called in Scotland?
options: *Hogmanay | Burns Night | Ceilidh | Eisteddfod
explanation: In Scotland, 31 December is called Hogmanay. For some Scottish people it is a bigger celebration than Christmas.

stem: What do people remember on Bonfire Night, 5 November?
options: *A failed plot to blow up Parliament in 1605 | The end of the First World War | The Battle of Hastings | The Great Fire of London
explanation: In 1605 a group of Catholics, including Guy Fawkes, tried to blow up the Houses of Parliament. People mark this with fireworks and bonfires.

stem: Why do many people wear poppies in early November?
options: *To remember people who died in wars | To celebrate the harvest | To mark the start of winter | To celebrate Guy Fawkes
explanation: Remembrance Day is 11 November. People wear red poppies to remember those who died fighting for the UK and its allies.

stem: When is Valentine's Day?
options: *14 February | 1 April | 14 March | 31 October
explanation: On Valentine's Day, 14 February, people send cards or gifts to someone they love.

stem: On 1 April, people traditionally play jokes on each other until midday.
options: *True | False
explanation: April Fool's Day is on 1 April. People play jokes on each other, but only until midday.

stem: Which TWO of these are Christian festivals?
options: *Easter | *Christmas | Diwali | Hanukkah
explanation: Christmas celebrates the birth of Jesus and Easter remembers his death and resurrection. Diwali is a Hindu and Sikh festival and Hanukkah is Jewish.

stem: On which date is Halloween?
options: *31 October | 1 November | 5 November | 11 November
explanation: Halloween is on 31 October. Children often dress up and go 'trick or treating'.

stem: Which food is traditionally from Scotland?
options: *Haggis | Yorkshire pudding | Welsh cakes | Ulster fry
explanation: Haggis is a traditional Scottish dish made from sheep's stomach stuffed with offal, oats and spices. It is often eaten on Burns Night.

stem: Which dish is traditionally linked to England?
options: *Roast beef with Yorkshire pudding | Haggis | Welsh cakes | Ulster fry
explanation: Roast beef, often served with Yorkshire pudding made from batter, is a traditional English meal.

stem: You need a TV licence to watch programmes on any device at the time they are broadcast.
options: *True | False
explanation: A TV licence is needed to watch or record live TV on any device, including a computer or phone. The money helps pay for the BBC.

stem: What are national parks?
options: *Protected areas of countryside that everyone can visit | Gardens owned by the monarch | Sports grounds for local teams | Private estates that are closed to visitors
explanation: National parks are areas of protected countryside. They are open to everyone for walking, camping and other activities.

stem: What is Big Ben?
options: *The great bell in the clock at the Houses of Parliament | The tower of Westminster Abbey | A large clock in Trafalgar Square | The main bell of St Paul's Cathedral
explanation: Big Ben is the nickname of the great bell in the clock tower at the Houses of Parliament. The tower was named Elizabeth Tower in 2012.

stem: In which county is the Eden Project, with its huge greenhouses of plants?
options: *Cornwall | Devon | Kent | Somerset
explanation: The Eden Project in Cornwall has large domes holding plants from around the world. It is also an educational charity.

stem: Where is the Giant's Causeway?
options: *Northern Ireland | Scotland | Wales | England
explanation: The Giant's Causeway is on the north-east coast of Northern Ireland. It is made of thousands of six-sided rock columns.

stem: Which national park contains Windermere, the largest lake in England?
options: *The Lake District | Snowdonia | The Peak District | Dartmoor
explanation: The Lake District is England's largest national park. Windermere is England's largest lake.

stem: What is the highest mountain in Wales?
options: *Snowdon (Yr Wyddfa) | Ben Nevis | Scafell Pike | Slieve Donard
explanation: Snowdon, also called Yr Wyddfa, is the highest mountain in Wales. Ben Nevis in Scotland is the highest in the UK.

stem: Loch Lomond, the largest area of fresh water in mainland Britain, is in which country?
options: *Scotland | Wales | England | Northern Ireland
explanation: Loch Lomond is in Scotland. It is part of the Loch Lomond and the Trossachs National Park.

stem: The London Eye is a large observation wheel on the south bank of the River Thames.
options: *True | False
explanation: The London Eye opened to mark the year 2000. From the top, visitors can see across much of London.

stem: Who is the patron saint of Scotland?
options: *St Andrew | St David | St George | St Patrick
explanation: St Andrew is the patron saint of Scotland and St Andrew's Day is 30 November. St David is for Wales, St George for England and St Patrick for Northern Ireland.

stem: When is St David's Day, the national day of Wales?
options: *1 March | 17 March | 23 April | 30 November
explanation: St David's Day is on 1 March. St Patrick's Day is 17 March, St George's Day is 23 April and St Andrew's Day is 30 November.

stem: When is St George's Day?
options: *23 April | 1 March | 17 March | 30 November
explanation: St George is the patron saint of England and his day is 23 April.

stem: Who is the head of the Church of England?
options: *The monarch | The Archbishop of Canterbury | The Prime Minister | The Pope
explanation: The monarch is the head of the Church of England. The Archbishop of Canterbury is its spiritual leader.

stem: People in the UK are free to choose any religion, or to have no religion.
options: *True | False
explanation: The UK has religious freedom. People can follow any faith, change their faith or have none.

stem: What is the national church in Scotland?
options: *The Church of Scotland | The Church of England | The Church in Wales | The Roman Catholic Church
explanation: The Church of Scotland is a Presbyterian church. It is run by ministers and elders, not by the monarch.

stem: Where is the Grand National horse race held?
options: *Aintree, near Liverpool | Ascot | Epsom | Newmarket
explanation: The Grand National is a famous horse race at Aintree, near Liverpool. Royal Ascot is another well-known race meeting.

stem: Which is the oldest tennis tournament in the world?
options: *Wimbledon | The US Open | The French Open | The Australian Open
explanation: The Wimbledon Championships began in 1877. It is the oldest tennis tournament in the world and the only major one played on grass.

stem: Which town in Scotland is known as the home of golf?
options: *St Andrews | Gleneagles | Inverness | Stirling
explanation: Golf has been played in Scotland since the 15th century. St Andrews is known around the world as the home of golf.

stem: Who was the first man to run a mile in under four minutes, in 1954?
options: *Sir Roger Bannister | Sir Steve Redgrave | Sir Chris Hoy | Sir Mo Farah
explanation: Sir Roger Bannister ran a mile in under four minutes in 1954. Nobody had done it before.

stem: How many times had London hosted the Olympic Games by 2012?
options: *Three | Two | One | Four
explanation: London hosted the Olympic Games in 1908, 1948 and 2012. The 2012 Games were held mainly in Stratford, east London.

stem: The Paralympic Games began from work at which hospital?
options: *Stoke Mandeville | Great Ormond Street | St Thomas' | Addenbrooke's
explanation: Sport for disabled people was developed at Stoke Mandeville hospital in Buckinghamshire. This work led to the Paralympic Games.

stem: Sir Steve Redgrave won rowing gold medals at five Olympic Games in a row.
options: *True | False
explanation: Sir Steve Redgrave won gold in rowing at five Olympic Games one after another, from 1984 to 2000.

stem: In which sport do England and Australia compete for The Ashes?
options: *Cricket | Rugby | Tennis | Golf
explanation: The Ashes is a famous series of cricket matches between England and Australia.

stem: What is the currency of the UK?
options: *The pound sterling | The euro | The dollar | The franc
explanation: The UK currency is the pound sterling. There are 100 pence in a pound.

stem: Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own banknotes, which can be used anywhere in the UK.
options: *True | False
explanation: Banks in Scotland and Northern Ireland print their own banknotes. They are valid everywhere in the UK, although some shops may not accept them.

stem: Which language is spoken by many people in Wales, alongside English?
options: *Welsh | Gaelic | Cornish | Manx
explanation: Many people in Wales speak Welsh, and children learn it at school. In parts of Scotland some people speak Gaelic.

stem: Women make up about half of the workforce in Britain today.
options: *True | False
explanation: Women in Britain have the same rights to work as men. Today they make up about half of the workforce.

stem: The UK constitution is written down in a single document.
options: True | *False
explanation: The UK constitution is not written in one document, so it is often called 'unwritten'. It comes from laws, conventions and court decisions.

stem: What type of monarchy does the UK have?
options: *A constitutional monarchy | An absolute monarchy | An elected monarchy | A military monarchy
explanation: In a constitutional monarchy the king or queen does not rule the country. The elected government makes decisions.

stem: Who is the head of state of the UK?
options: *The monarch | The Prime Minister | The Speaker of the House of Commons | The Lord Chancellor
explanation: The monarch is the head of state. The Prime Minister is the head of the government.

stem: What does the Speaker of the House of Commons do?
options: *Chairs debates and keeps order, staying neutral | Leads the government | Speaks for the monarch | Leads the opposition
explanation: The Speaker is an MP chosen by other MPs. The Speaker chairs debates, keeps order and does not take sides.

stem: Who sits in the House of Commons?
options: *Members of Parliament elected by voters | Peers appointed for life | Senior judges | Bishops of the Church of England
explanation: The House of Commons is made up of MPs elected by voters in their constituencies. It is the more important of the two Houses.

stem: Which TWO kinds of member sit in the House of Lords?
options: *Life peers | *Senior bishops of the Church of England | Elected MPs | Local councillors
explanation: Members of the House of Lords are not elected. They include life peers, some hereditary peers and senior bishops of the Church of England.

stem: How often must a general election be held?
options: *At least every five years | Every four years | Every three years | Every seven years
explanation: A general election must be held at least every five years. MPs are elected in every constituency.

stem: What is the minimum age to vote in a UK general election?
explanation: You must be 18 or over to vote in elections to the UK Parliament. In some elections in Scotland and Wales, people can vote at 16.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: In which year did the voting age for everyone become 18?
explanation: The voting age was lowered from 21 to 18 for men and women in 1969.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: In the 1830s and 1840s, the Chartists campaigned for every man to have the right to vote.
options: *True | False
explanation: The Chartists were a group who campaigned for political reform, including votes for every man and secret ballots.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: What is the Prime Minister's official home in London?
options: *10 Downing Street | 11 Downing Street | Buckingham Palace | Lambeth Palace
explanation: The Prime Minister lives and works at 10 Downing Street. The Prime Minister also has a country house called Chequers.

stem: Which government minister is responsible for the economy?
options: *The Chancellor of the Exchequer | The Home Secretary | The Foreign Secretary | The Lord Chancellor
explanation: The Chancellor of the Exchequer is responsible for the economy. The Home Secretary deals with crime, policing and immigration.

stem: What is the second-largest party in the House of Commons usually called?
options: *The opposition | The cabinet | The civil service | The coalition
explanation: The second-largest party is the opposition. Its leader is the Leader of the Opposition, who leads a shadow cabinet.

stem: Civil servants must be politically neutral.
options: *True | False
explanation: Civil servants carry out government policy. They do not take sides and keep working for the new government after an election.

stem: What is the official record of what is said in Parliament called?
options: *Hansard | The Domesday Book | The Gazette | The Magna Carta
explanation: Hansard is the official report of what is said in Parliament. Anyone can read it, and debates are also broadcast.

stem: Where does the Northern Ireland Assembly meet?
options: *Stormont, in Belfast | Holyrood, in Edinburgh | Westminster, in London | Cardiff Bay, in Cardiff
explanation: The Northern Ireland Assembly meets at Stormont in Belfast. It has powers over matters such as health and education.

stem: Where is the Scottish Parliament?
options: *Holyrood, in Edinburgh | Glasgow city centre | Stormont, in Belfast | Westminster, in London
explanation: The Scottish Parliament meets at Holyrood in Edinburgh. It can make laws for Scotland on many matters.

stem: The UK is a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council.
options: *True | False
explanation: The UK is one of five permanent members of the UN Security Council, which works to keep international peace and security.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The UK and international institutions

stem: What is the Commonwealth?
options: *An association of countries, most once part of the British Empire | A group of European countries that trade freely | A military alliance of North Atlantic countries | The parliament of the four UK countries
explanation: The Commonwealth is a voluntary association of countries. Most were once part of the British Empire, and the monarch is its head.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The UK and international institutions

stem: What is NATO?
options: *A group of countries that agree to defend each other | A group of countries that share one currency | A charity that helps refugees | A court that settles trade disputes
explanation: The UK is a member of NATO, a group of European and North American countries that have agreed to help each other if they are attacked.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The UK and international institutions

stem: Which organisation created the European Convention on Human Rights?
options: *The Council of Europe | The United Nations | The Commonwealth | NATO
explanation: The Council of Europe created the European Convention on Human Rights. It is separate from the European Union.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The UK and international institutions

stem: Who usually hears cases in a magistrates' court in England and Wales?
options: *Magistrates, who are usually unpaid volunteers | A judge and a jury | Police officers | Members of Parliament
explanation: Most minor criminal cases are heard by magistrates. They are usually unpaid and do not need legal qualifications.

stem: How many people sit on a jury in England, Wales and Northern Ireland?
explanation: A jury has 12 people in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. In Scotland a jury has 15 people.

stem: In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, which court hears cases against people aged 10 to 17?
options: *A youth court | The Crown Court | A county court | The small claims court
explanation: Young people aged 10 to 17 accused of a crime are usually tried in a youth court. Scotland uses a Children's Hearings System.

stem: Which TWO of these are criminal offences in the UK?
options: *Carrying a weapon in public | *Selling tobacco to someone under 18 | Not paying back a loan to a friend | Breaking a contract with a builder
explanation: Carrying a weapon and selling tobacco to under-18s are crimes. Unpaid debts and broken contracts are usually settled under civil law.

stem: A disagreement about faulty goods bought from a shop is usually dealt with under civil law.
options: *True | False
explanation: Civil law covers disputes between people or businesses, such as faulty goods, debts and housing. Criminal law covers crimes.

stem: What do Police and Crime Commissioners (PCCs) do?
options: *Make sure local police are run well | Decide sentences in court | Write new criminal laws | Train police officers
explanation: PCCs are elected by the public in police areas in England and Wales. They set local police priorities and make sure policing is effective.

stem: Forcing someone to marry is a criminal offence in the UK.
options: *True | False
explanation: A forced marriage is one where someone does not agree to it. It is a crime, and courts can also issue orders to protect people at risk.

stem: People on the electoral register can be asked to serve on a jury.
options: *True | False
explanation: If you are on the electoral register you may be chosen for jury service. You must do it unless you have a good reason.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: What is the electoral register?
options: *The official list of people who can vote | A list of everyone who pays tax | A record of all MPs | A list of council employees
explanation: To vote, your name must be on the electoral register. You can register online or through your local council.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: What does National Insurance help pay for?
options: *State benefits and services such as the State Pension | Car insurance | Home insurance against fire | Private health care
explanation: National Insurance contributions help pay for state benefits and services, such as the State Pension and the NHS.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: What is the minimum age to drive a car on UK roads?
explanation: You must be at least 17 to drive a car. You need a driving licence, which you get after passing a driving test.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community
